📖 Column Reference Guide

📊 Status — 200-Week Moving Average

Ranks each stock by how far its current price sits above or below its 200-Week Moving Average (200-WMA) — the average closing price over the last ~4 years. Stocks near or below their 200-WMA have historically offered the strongest long-term entry points.

🔴 Deep Value >10% below the 200-WMA. Historically rare. The stock has dropped well below its long-term average — highest potential upside, but worth understanding why it fell.
🟠 Undervalued 3–10% below the 200-WMA. Prime buy territory per the strategy — price is approaching its long-term average from below.
🟢 Buy Zone Within ±3% of the 200-WMA. The ideal entry point — price is right at its long-term average, the sweet spot of the strategy.
🟡 Watchlist 3–15% above the 200-WMA. Quality stock trading above its average — add to your watchlist and wait for a pullback to Buy Zone or below.
⬜ Extended >15% above the 200-WMA. Overextended — the stock has run far above its average. Patience required; a better entry will likely come.
📉 P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings)

How much investors pay for each $1 of annual profit. A stock at $50 earning $5/share has a P/E of 10x. Lower generally = cheaper relative to earnings. Uses trailing 12-month P/E; falls back to forward P/E when unavailable.

<15x Value territory. Cheap relative to earnings. Common in mature, slow-growth industries. May signal an undervalued opportunity — or a declining business.
15–25x Fair value. The historical average for the S&P 500. Reasonable pricing for a stable, profitable company with moderate growth.
25–40x Growth premium. Investors are paying up for expected future earnings growth. Justified if the company is expanding fast; risky if growth disappoints.
>40x Expensive. Very high expectations baked in. Earnings must grow substantially to justify the price — elevated risk if the growth story falters.
— Not available. Company is unprofitable (negative earnings make P/E meaningless), or data is unavailable from the data source.
📐 Fib Zone (Fibonacci Retracement)

Measures how far a stock has pulled back from its 52-week high. The key Fibonacci levels — 38.2%, 50%, and 61.8% — tend to act as natural support zones during an uptrend. Hover any badge for the exact 52-week high, low, and retracement %.

🎯 61.8% — Golden Ratio Strongest level. Derived from the golden ratio (1.618) — the most-watched Fibonacci support. Major reversals most often occur here during an uptrend. Highest-conviction entry of the three.
🎯 50.0% — Midpoint Psychological level. Not a true Fibonacci number, but traders widely treat the halfway point of a move as key support/resistance. Broadly followed and self-reinforcing.
🎯 38.2% — Shallow Strong trend signal. A modest pullback — bulls stepped in early. Indicates a robust uptrend. Least downside risk of the three key levels, but also least upside if the trend stalls.
📐 Golden Zone 38.2–61.8% range. Price is inside the golden zone but not pinned to a specific level. Still a favorable area — most traders consider the full 38.2–61.8% band the primary buy zone in an uptrend.
— 23.6% / 78.6% Minor Fib levels. 23.6% = very shallow pullback (powerful, fast-moving trend). 78.6% = deep retracement (trend under pressure — watch for a breakdown below the swing low).
~xx% Between levels. Price is not near any key Fibonacci level. No actionable Fib signal at this time — consider other indicators or wait for price to reach a level.
Other notes: Click any stock row to expand its price chart · † = fewer than 200 weeks of price data (200-WMA is an approximation) · 👑 Crown = Dividend Aristocrat or King — 25+ consecutive years of dividend increases (e.g. KO, JNJ, PG) · Yes = pays a dividend · No = no dividend · Data via Yahoo Finance (yfinance) · Not financial advice.
